introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; publicités, filigranes gcerevision.com et mention manuscrite d'adresse web ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée ; les effectifs sont donnés en ordres de grandeur prudents (« roughly nine to ten million », « about two million »).

Question 2 : l'énoncé imprimé associe « the Jihad in Futa Jallon » aux dates 1854-1864. Ces dates correspondent à la guerre sainte d'Al-Hajj Umar Tall (empire toucouleur, parti de Dinguiraye, en bordure du Fouta-Djalon), alors que le jihad du Fouta-Djalon proprement dit date d'environ 1725 (Karamoko Alfa). Le sujet est recopié tel quel ; le corrigé signale la divergence et traite le mouvement de 1854-1864, avec le jihad du Fouta-Djalon en arrière-plan. L'année de début de la guerre sainte d'Umar est donnée de façon prudente (1852 ou 1854 selon les sources).

Question 2 : détails à vérifier par un historien (siège de Médine en 1857, prise de Ségou en 1861 et de Hamdallahi en 1862, mort d'Umar en 1864, chute de Ségou face à Archinard en 1890) ; ils sont cités conformément à l'historiographie courante, mais le corrigé ne s'appuie pas sur des chiffres.

Question 7 : les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, invitation des « Immortal Seven » et acquittement des sept évêques le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre) ; le corrigé précise le choix du calendrier julien.
Question 4 : le massacre de Thiaroye (décembre 1944), les émeutes d'Accra (1948) et la conférence de Brazzaville (1944) sont cités sans bilan chiffré, le nombre exact de victimes étant discuté.

Question 5 : exemples de coups d'État (Togo 1963, Ghana 1966, Nigeria 1966, Ouganda 1971, Éthiopie 1974, Mali 2020) cités sans chiffres ; la formule « very many people were killed » remplace volontairement tout bilan sous Amin, très discuté.

Question 12 : la liste des suspensions et départs (Nigeria 1995, Fidji, Zimbabwe 2003, Gambie 2013 puis retour 2018) et l'adhésion du Cameroun en 1995 sont citées de mémoire historique ; aucun chiffre financier n'est avancé.

Questions à thème régional : les noms de thèmes sont qualifiés (par exemple `military coups in africa`, `refugee crisis in africa`, `league of nations`) pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone ; à reverifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine the reasons for the failure of African resistance to European occupation of the African continent in the late 19th century.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Between about 1880 and 1900 European powers occupied almost the whole of Africa in what is known as the Scramble for Africa, whose rules were framed at the Berlin Conference of 1884-85 (including the principle of "effective occupation"). Africans resisted in many forms: armed resistance by states such as the Zulu, the Asante, Samori Toure's state, the Mahdist state and the Ndebele, as well as diplomacy, flight and guerrilla war. Most of these resistance movements failed, and the reasons were military, political, economic and diplomatic.

**1. European military superiority.**
- European armies had breech-loading rifles, repeating rifles, artillery and especially the Maxim machine gun (invented in 1884), which could destroy massed African formations. Examples include the Ndebele defeat in 1893 and the Mahdist defeat at Omdurman in 1898, where Kitchener's army with Maxim guns and gunboats won a decisive victory.
- Steamships and gunboats made rivers such as the Niger and the Nile routes of conquest, and the use of quinine reduced deaths of Europeans from malaria, making inland campaigns more feasible.
- European armies had training, discipline, supply lines and often African auxiliaries (for example the tirailleurs sénégalais in French service, and local allies).

**2. African disunity and the exploitation of rivalries.**
- Africans were divided into many states, ethnic groups and religious groups, and old rivalries were used by Europeans through divide-and-rule: allies and rival groups were recruited as soldiers or guides against each other.
- Some African rulers, such as Lobengula in his dealings with Rhodes (Rudd Concession 1888), or the Duala chiefs in the Cameroon treaties of 1884, were persuaded to sign treaties whose real effects they did not understand or whose terms were later interpreted in a European way.
- Succession disputes, as in Buganda or between members of royal families, weakened resistance.

**3. Weaknesses in African strategy and resources.**
- Many states relied on traditional weapons, a few imported guns of old design and tactics of open battle, which were suited to local wars but not to modern European firepower. Samori Toure, who obtained modern rifles and reorganised his army, resisted the French for about sixteen years, but he lacked supplies and was captured in 1898.
- African states often could not produce modern weapons or ammunition and depended on supplies through the coast, which Europeans could blockade.
- Natural disasters such as the rinderpest epidemic of the 1890s, which killed cattle in eastern and southern Africa, as well as famine and disease, weakened some societies.

**4. Diplomatic and legal factors.** European powers agreed among themselves at Berlin and in later treaties how to partition Africa, so that African states could not exploit rivalries among them for long. The principle of effective occupation encouraged rapid military campaigns.

**5. Exceptions that prove the rule.** Ethiopia under Menelik II defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896 because it was united under a strong ruler, had imported large numbers of modern rifles and artillery, used diplomacy skilfully and had good leadership. Where such conditions were absent, resistance failed.

**Conclusion.** African resistance failed mainly because of the gap in military technology, reinforced by disunity, lack of modern equipment and the skill with which Europeans exploited rivalries. The most important single reason was the superiority in weapons and organisation, but this advantage was multiplied by political divisions among Africans. Resistance was not wasted: it showed African agency, delayed colonisation in places, and inspired later nationalism.
